title: Inflammation as a coordinated program
objective: Explain inflammation as a cytokine-coordinated program and how it reaches sensory neurons.

steps.title: The classic signs, explained
steps.body:
Inflammation's four classic signs, redness, heat, swelling and pain, come from a coordinated program:

- vessels dilate and leak (redness, heat, swelling)
- cells are recruited by chemokines
- mediators sensitize nerve endings (pain)

Cytokines (B3-L1) orchestrate the timing and the cast.

steps.title: The inflammatory soup meets the nerve ending
steps.body:
Damaged and immune cells release a mix, protons, ATP, bradykinin, prostaglandins, cytokines, often called the 'inflammatory soup.'

Many of these act on receptors on sensory endings, lowering their threshold so they fire to weaker stimuli. That's **peripheral sensitization** (A9), the link between an immune event and a change in what you feel.

visual.alt: A sensory nerve ending surrounded by inflammatory mediators (protons, ATP, prostaglandins, cytokines); its firing threshold drops and it fires more spikes to the same stimulus.
visual.caption: Mediators lower the ending's threshold, so a gentle stimulus now fires it.

steps.prompt: Match each inflammatory feature to its cause.
pairs: Vessel dilation and increased blood flow
Leaky vessels let fluid into tissue
steps.explanation: Each cardinal sign maps onto a specific cellular event, and the pain sign is literally neuroimmune.

steps.prompt: Inflamed skin hurts when gently touched (normally painless). At the receptor level, what changed?
options: The skin's touch neurons were deleted during the inflammation
Inflammatory mediators lowered the endings' threshold to gentle touch
The inflamed skin grew new bone that presses on the nerves
The brain stopped working and now misreads every signal as pain
steps.explanation: Lowered thresholds mean normally sub-threshold stimuli now fire the neuron, producing tenderness (allodynia). This is sensitization driven by immune mediators (A9).

steps.setup: You think a specific cytokine drives the tenderness in an inflamed tissue.
steps.prompt: Sketch one experiment to test whether that cytokine is necessary.
steps.reveal: Options: block the cytokine or its receptor (neutralizing antibody, receptor antagonist, or genetic knockout) and test whether tenderness is reduced; conversely, apply the cytokine alone and see if it produces tenderness (sufficiency). Necessity + sufficiency together make the strongest case, the same logic as the sensory knockout/activation experiments in Track A.

reviewNotes: Confidence medium. Textbook-level; bridges to A9 and B7.
